newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile industry upbeat as Mercosur tariffs tumble.
newsitem.headline: Chile industry upbeat as Mercosur tariffs tumble.

text.p: Chilean industry expects exports to Latin America's Southern Cone to boom as a free-trade accord between Chile and the Mercosur bloc went into effect Tuesday, slashing tariffs, said officials.
"For Chilean industry, this agreement is crucial," said Hugo Baierlein, foreign trade manager at industry lobby group Sociedad de Fomento Fabril (Sofofa).
"Our industry is highly competitive and can now enter the Mercosur markets on good terms," he said.

The agreement, approved by the Chilean Congress last month, will give the country's manufacturers easier access to the 200 million consumers who live in the four Mercosur member countries: Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

"It is a great opportunity...and will give Chilean products access to a much wider market," said Carlos Vicuna, general manager of copper products maker Madeco, which already has investments in Argentina.
Chilean exports to the Mercosur have surged in recent years and totalled $1.8 billion last year, up 30 percent from 1994.
Although exports to the bloc account for just 11 percent of Chile's total, a large portion of the Mercosur trade is in higher-value manufactured goods rather than commodities.

"Around one third of the exports are manufactured. This is not the same as with exports to NAFTA (Canada, Mexico and the United States) or the European Union, which are mainly raw materials," said Baierlein.
Business leaders expect to see a boom in Mercosur exports from the textile, footware, furniture and chemical industries, he said.
The main opposition to the agreement, which took years to negotiate, came from farmers who fear they will be overwhelmed by a flood of cheap grain from Brazil and Argentina.
"Certain areas of traditional agriculture including sugar, wheat and rice will be hurt. The Mercosur countries are much more efficient in these areas than us," said Baierlein.
The accord, which was signed by the presidents of the five countries in June, erased some tariffs immediately, with others falling over the next eight years.
Tariffs on a few politically sensitive items, such as wheat and rice, will stay in force for up to a further 10 years.
